issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The profile is for a male patient with police trauma, but two trigger items and the body-shame appraisal are specifically sexual-trauma themed. That is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type unless there is an additional sexual trauma history, which is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

This makes the selected items clinically incoherent as a single trauma-linked PTSD profile.

issues.explanation: For a police trauma in a 47-year-old male bus driver, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is hard to reconcile unless the index event involved sexual assault or exposure to sexual violence in a highly personal way; nothing else in the profile supports that specificity.

issues.explanation: Body-focused shame is more characteristic of sexual assault or severe bodily violation. In this profile it does not cohere with the police trauma framing, and it is reinforced only by the sexual-trauma-specific trigger, creating an implausible subtheme not supported by the rest of the nodes.

vignette: Six years ago, Marcus Thorne was driving Route 14 through a heavy downpour when a passenger aboard lost control, swinging a metal water bottle at a sleeping commuter. Marcus had to break a two-armed hold around his neck to intervene, pressing the man to the floor until his breathing slowed. The police arrived three minutes later, sirens cutting through the rain, and in the confusion, the officers tackled Marcus anyway, assuming he was the aggressor. He spent four hours in a holding cell before they reviewed the dashcam footage and released him. What frightened him most was how quickly his own efforts had been read as a threat, how the uniforms that were supposed to bring safety had instead confirmed his suspicion that the world is a dangerous place. Over the following months, he developed a rhythm of checking the apartment door and windows, turning each deadbolt and latch multiple times until the metal clicked into place. He felt untethered from the cultural gatherings and familiar faces of his neighborhood, a hollowed-out sense of disconnection that simply was. When colleagues asked what had happened, he would find himself speaking about the incident and quickly stop, realizing how easily the words had slipped out. Marcus returned to driving, but the first time a marked cruiser fell in behind his bus, a memory of the event came to mind suddenly, absolute and unbidden. He brought both hands up to cover his face, hiding behind them until the cruiser pulled away. He began avoiding other people on his route, leaning forward over the steering wheel, keeping his eyes fixed on the road and refusing to meet the gaze of anyone who boarded. On his lunch breaks, he sat in the depot bathroom with the radio turned so loud it rattled the metal stall doors, using the volume to occupy his senses. Irritability settled into his days, surfacing as sharp outbursts when a passenger questioned his routing or a supervisor asked about his missed stops; his concentration slipped during long stretches, and his hands kept drifting to his face whenever any authority figure appeared. He was certain that no one would believe him if he explained his side of things; people could not be trusted to see what had actually happened. The habits hardened over weeks and months. At home, the television became his constant companion, filling the apartment so he would not have to sit with the silence. He stopped returning calls from his sister, keeping his distance while the anger that sometimes leaked out of him without warning remained. At work, he requested temporary transfers away from routes near police stations, but the depot manager noted his declining attendance and the growing tension with his fellow drivers. What finally brought Marcus to the clinic was a morning when he realized he could no longer complete his run without feeling his pulse spike at the sight of any marked vehicle, and he feared he would lose his license altogether. He hopes to find a way to sit in his bus again without covering his face or waiting for the loud music to save him, though he worries that seeking help might only mean being asked to talk about the event until he has to do it all over again.
